q: Backflush costing, used in just-in-time environments, is a system under which:

options.A: Costs are charged to each job daily through detailed stores and labour records
options.B: A separate work-in-progress account is maintained for every operation in the factory
options.C: Product costs are applied (flushed back) to the units produced only at the completion or sale stage, using predetermined rates, with little or no detailed tracking of work-in-progress
options.D: Overheads are never charged to production at all

e: Backflush costing suits just-in-time production where work-in-progress is minimal, so costs are flushed back to finished units only at completion or sale using predetermined rates, without detailed tracking of work-in-progress at each stage.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Target costing works mainly before production begins, at the design and planning stage, to close the gap between the estimated cost and the allowable target cost.
2. Kaizen costing works during the production stage, seeking small, continuous reductions in the actual cost of manufacturing a product already in production.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: Both 1 and 2
options.B: 1 only
options.C: 2 only
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Target costing is a pre-production, design-stage technique that sets an allowable cost from price minus desired profit, while kaizen costing operates during production to achieve small continuous cost reductions, so both statements are correct.

q: Environmental costing is concerned with:

options.A: Costing only the landscaping and gardening expenses of a factory
options.B: Identifying costs such as waste treatment and disposal, effluent control, environmental compliance and clean-up, which are often hidden in general overheads, and assigning them to the products and processes that cause them
options.C: Excluding all pollution-control expenditure from the cost of production
options.D: Valuing natural resources owned by the Government

e: Environmental costs like waste treatment, effluent control, compliance and clean-up are often buried in general overheads; environmental costing identifies them separately and assigns them to the products and processes that cause them.

q: Under the Prevention–Appraisal–Failure (PAF) classification of quality costs, the cost of handling customer complaints, warranty repairs and goods returned after sale is classified as:

options.A: Prevention cost
options.B: Appraisal cost
options.C: Internal failure cost
options.D: External failure cost

e: Costs arising after sale, such as handling customer complaints, warranty repairs and goods returned, are external failure costs under the PAF model, because the failure is detected only after the product reaches the customer.

q: The learning curve effect in costing refers to the phenomenon that:

options.A: Workers become slower as they repeat a task over a long period
options.B: The total cost of production always rises in direct proportion to output
options.C: As the cumulative quantity of a product doubles, the cumulative average time (and cost) per unit falls by a constant percentage, as workers gain experience and efficiency
options.D: Fixed costs per unit fall as output rises within the existing capacity

e: The learning curve states that as cumulative output doubles, the cumulative average time and cost per unit fall by a constant percentage, because workers gain experience, speed and efficiency with repetition.

q: The first unit of a new product takes 100 labour hours. The learning rate is 80%. The total labour time required to produce the first 4 units in all is:

options.A: 256 hours
options.B: 320 hours
options.C: 400 hours
options.D: 200 hours

e: At 80 percent learning, cumulative average time is 100 hours for 1 unit, 80 hours for 2 units and 64 hours for 4 units, so total time for 4 units = 64 x 4 = 256 hours.

q: An enterprise shows sales of Rs 4,00,000 with a profit of Rs 20,000 in one year and sales of Rs 6,00,000 with a profit of Rs 70,000 in the next year. The P/V ratio is:
e: P/V ratio = change in profit divided by change in sales x 100 = (70000 - 20000) / (600000 - 400000) x 100 = 50000 / 200000 x 100 = 25 percent.

q: A product sells for Rs 150 per unit with a variable cost of Rs 90 per unit. Fixed costs are Rs 4,80,000. The number of units that must be sold to earn a desired profit of Rs 20 per unit is:

options.A: 8,000 units
options.B: 16,000 units
options.C: 6,000 units
options.D: 12,000 units

e: Contribution per unit = 150 - 90 = Rs 60. Required sales: 60 x units = 480000 + 20 x units, so 40 x units = 480000 and units = 12000.

q: The total cost of producing 20,000 units is Rs 6,00,000 and that of producing 25,000 units is Rs 7,10,000, all other conditions remaining the same. The differential cost of the additional 5,000 units, per unit, is:
e: Differential cost = 710000 - 600000 = Rs 110000 for 5000 extra units, so differential cost per unit = 110000 / 5000 = Rs 22.00.

q: A factory has 9,000 machine hours available. Product A gives a contribution of Rs 90 per unit, takes 3 machine hours per unit and has a maximum demand of 2,000 units. Product B gives a contribution of Rs 50 per unit and takes 2 machine hours per unit, its demand being unlimited. Machine hours are the limiting factor. The maximum total contribution obtainable is:
e: Contribution per machine hour: A = 90 / 3 = Rs 30, B = 50 / 2 = Rs 25, so A is preferred. A uses 2000 x 3 = 6000 hours giving Rs 180000; remaining 3000 hours give 1500 units of B giving Rs 75000; total = Rs 255000.

q: A firm with spare capacity receives an export order for 3,000 units at Rs 85 per unit. Its variable cost is Rs 70 per unit and accepting the order will involve additional export packing of Rs 5 per unit, but no extra fixed cost; domestic sales will not be affected. The correct decision is to:

options.A: Reject the order, as it results in a loss of Rs 30,000
options.B: Accept the order, as it yields an additional contribution of Rs 30,000
options.C: Accept the order, as it yields an additional contribution of Rs 45,000
options.D: Reject the order, because the export price is below the normal domestic price

e: Incremental contribution per unit = 85 - 70 - 5 = Rs 10, so total gain = 10 x 3000 = Rs 30000 with no extra fixed cost and no loss of domestic sales, hence the order should be accepted.

q: In a break-even chart, a wider angle of incidence at the break-even point indicates that:

options.A: The firm will make losses at all levels of sales
options.B: The rate at which profit grows beyond the break-even point is lower
options.C: The angle has no connection with profitability
options.D: The P/V ratio is higher, so that profits increase more steeply once sales pass the break-even point

e: The angle of incidence is the angle between the sales line and the total cost line at the break-even point; a wider angle means a higher P/V ratio, so profit grows more steeply beyond break-even.

q: Last year a firm spent Rs 2,00,000 on a market survey for a proposed new product. It is now deciding whether to launch the product. For this decision, the amount already spent on the survey should be:

options.A: Added to the fixed costs of the new product
options.B: Recovered by raising the selling price of the product
options.C: Ignored, being a sunk cost already incurred which will not change whichever alternative is chosen
options.D: Treated as the opportunity cost of launching the product

e: The Rs 200000 already spent on the market survey cannot be recovered or altered by the launch decision, so it is a sunk cost and must be ignored in appraising whether to launch.

q: A firm proposes to use its own vacant godown for a new product line. The godown could otherwise be let out for a rent of Rs 40,000 per month. In appraising the new line, the rent forgone is:

options.A: An opportunity cost of using the godown, to be taken into account in the appraisal
options.B: A sunk cost, because the godown was purchased many years ago
options.C: Irrelevant, because no cash payment is actually made for the godown
options.D: A fixed cost already included in last year's accounts

e: Rent of Rs 40000 per month forgone by using the vacant godown in-house is a benefit sacrificed for the new line, hence it is an opportunity cost to be charged in the appraisal even though no cash is paid.

q: Budgeted sales of a product are 5,000 units, while actual sales are 5,200 units. The standard profit (margin) is Rs 30 per unit. The sales volume variance, on the margin basis, is:

options.A: Rs 6,000 (Adverse)
options.B: Rs 6,000 (Favourable)
options.C: Rs 1,56,000 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 1,50,000 (Favourable)

e: Sales volume variance on margin basis = (actual quantity - budgeted quantity) x standard profit per unit = (5200 - 5000) x 30 = Rs 6000 Favourable.

q: In a DCF appraisal where cash flows are explicitly forecast only for the first few years of a long-lived project, the 'terminal value' (continuing value) added at the end of the forecast period represents:

options.A: The book value of the assets as on that date
options.B: The estimated worth, as at that date, of all the cash flows expected beyond the forecast period
options.C: The salvage value of the plant alone
options.D: The total undiscounted cash flows of the forecast period

e: Terminal value is the value placed at the end of the explicit forecast period to capture the worth at that date of all cash flows expected beyond the forecast period in a long-lived project.

q: A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 4,80,000. It is expected to yield net cash inflows of Rs 2,50,000 at the end of Year 1 and Rs 2,50,000 at the end of Year 2, besides a salvage value of Rs 80,000 at the end of Year 2. The present value factors at 10% are 0.909 for Year 1 and 0.826 for Year 2. The Net Present Value of the project is:

A project requires plant costing Rs 10,00,000 and additional working capital of Rs 1,50,000 at the start. It yields net cash inflows of Rs 3,00,000 at the end of each of the next 5 years, and the working capital is fully recovered at the end of Year 5. The cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 5 years at 10% is 3.791 and the present value factor for Year 5 is 0.621. The Net Present Value of the project is:
e: Initial outlay = 1000000 + 150000 = Rs 1150000. PV of inflows = 300000 x 3.791 = Rs 1137300 plus working capital recovery 150000 x 0.621 = Rs 93150, total Rs 1230450. NPV = 1230450 - 1150000 = plus Rs 80450.

q: A project plant carries annual depreciation of Rs 90,000 and the tax rate is 40%. The annual tax shield (tax saving) provided by the depreciation is:
e: Depreciation tax shield = depreciation x tax rate = 90000 x 40 percent = Rs 36000 saved in tax every year.

q: In Discounted Cash Flow appraisal, depreciation charged on the project's assets is not itself deducted as a cash outflow, because:

options.A: Depreciation is a non-cash charge; it affects the appraisal only through the tax saving (tax shield) it creates
options.B: The project's assets are never depreciated during their life
options.C: Depreciation is always exactly equal to the salvage value of the assets
options.D: Cash flows in DCF appraisal are stated after depreciation in all cases

e: Depreciation is a non-cash book charge involving no cash outflow, so it is not deducted in DCF; it enters the appraisal only through the tax saving, or tax shield, that it generates.

q: A post-completion audit of a major work is most usefully carried out:

options.A: Before the work is sanctioned, as a part of its feasibility study
options.B: Only in those cases where the cost overrun exceeds 10% of the sanctioned cost
options.C: After the work has been in operation long enough for its actual earnings and working expenses to be observed, so that the out-turn can be compared with the justification and lessons drawn for future estimates
options.D: By the contractor who executed the work, as a part of the completion report

e: A post-completion audit is useful only after the work has operated long enough for actual earnings and working expenses to be observed, so the out-turn can be compared with the original justification and lessons drawn.

q: Which of the following is an essential element of the financial justification note accompanying a railway work proposal?

options.A: The names of the officers who will supervise the execution of the work
options.B: The completion report of a similar work executed earlier
options.C: The list of stores indents to be placed for the materials required
options.D: The basis of the traffic and earnings projections, the anticipated additional working expenses, and the resulting net return on the estimated cost

e: A financial justification note must state the basis of traffic and earnings projections, the anticipated additional working expenses, and the resulting net return on the estimated cost of the work.

q: The Block Account of a railway records:

options.A: The daily cash balance of the railway with the Reserve Bank
options.B: The capital expenditure incurred, classified by assets, which together constitutes the capital-at-charge of the railway
options.C: The revenue expenditure of the railway under each Demand
options.D: The outstanding balances under Traffic Suspense

e: The Block Account records capital expenditure classified by assets; together these asset balances constitute the capital-at-charge of the railway.

q: In appraising a project, dividend payments made out of the project's profits are excluded from the project's cash outflows because:

options.A: Dividends are a distribution (appropriation) of the profit earned, that is, a financing flow, and not a cost of generating the project's cash flows
options.B: Dividends are never paid on capital invested in projects
options.C: Dividends are already included in the depreciation charge of the project
options.D: A project is assumed to earn no profit during its life

e: Dividends are an appropriation and distribution of profit already earned, that is a financing flow to capital providers, not a cost of generating project cash flows, so they are excluded from project appraisal.

q: The nominal (money) rate of return required on a project is 16% per annum and the expected rate of inflation is 6% per annum. The real rate of return, computed as (1.16 / 1.06 - 1), is approximately:
e: Real rate = (1.16 / 1.06) - 1 = 1.0943 - 1 = 0.0943, that is approximately 9.43 percent, after removing the effect of 6 percent inflation from the 16 percent nominal rate.

q: A limitation of the risk-adjusted discount rate method of handling risk in project appraisal is that:

options.A: It cannot be used along with the Net Present Value method
options.B: It ignores the risk of the project altogether
options.C: It applies a lower discount rate to a riskier project
options.D: By compounding a single risk premium over the whole life of the project, it in effect assumes that risk grows at a steady compound rate with time, penalising the distant cash flows increasingly

e: A risk-adjusted discount rate compounds one risk premium over the entire project life, implicitly assuming risk grows at a steady compound rate with time and thus penalising distant cash flows increasingly heavily.

q: A project with a long life and uniform annual cash inflows has a payback period of 4 years. Its payback reciprocal (1 / payback period) suggests an approximate internal rate of return of:
e: Payback reciprocal = 1 / payback period = 1 / 4 = 0.25, that is 25 percent, which approximates the IRR for a long-lived project with uniform annual inflows.

q: An investment of Rs 7,00,000 has an expected salvage value of Rs 1,00,000 at the end of its life and is expected to yield an average annual profit (after depreciation and tax) of Rs 60,000. The Average Rate of Return computed on the average investment is:
e: Average investment = (700000 + 100000) / 2 = Rs 400000. Average rate of return = 60000 / 400000 x 100 = 15 percent.

q: The crossover (Fisher) rate in capital budgeting is the discount rate at which:

options.A: The Net Present Value of a project is at its maximum
options.B: The Net Present Values of two competing projects are equal, so that their NPV ranking reverses on either side of that rate
options.C: The internal rate of return of a project equals its payback period
options.D: The Profitability Index of both the projects is zero

e: The crossover or Fisher rate is the discount rate at which the NPVs of two competing projects are equal, so their NPV ranking reverses on either side of that rate.

q: The Modified Internal Rate of Return (MIRR) of a project differs from the ordinary Internal Rate of Return in that under MIRR:

options.A: The cash inflows of the project are ignored altogether
options.B: No discounting or compounding of cash flows is done
options.C: Multiple rates of return always arise for every project
options.D: The intermediate cash inflows are compounded forward at the cost of capital, instead of at the IRR itself, removing the unrealistic reinvestment assumption and the multiple-IRR problem

e: MIRR compounds intermediate inflows forward at the cost of capital rather than at the IRR itself, removing the unrealistic reinvestment assumption of IRR and avoiding the multiple-IRR problem.

q: A work is expected to yield a net saving of Rs 45,000 every year indefinitely. At a discount rate of 10%, the present value of this perpetual annual saving (annual saving / discount rate) is:
e: Present value of a perpetuity = annual saving / discount rate = 45000 / 0.10 = Rs 450000.

q: Where projects are divisible and funds are limited for a single period (capital rationing), ranking the projects by their Profitability Index and accepting them in that order is used because it:

options.A: Maximises the speed with which the outlay is paid back
options.B: Dispenses with the need to compute the Net Present Value
options.C: Maximises the Net Present Value obtained per rupee of the scarce capital outlay
options.D: Ensures that every proposed project is at least partly accepted

e: Under single-period capital rationing with divisible projects, ranking by Profitability Index maximises the NPV obtained per rupee of the scarce capital outlay.

q: A project has expected net cash inflows with a mean of Rs 1,20,000 and a standard deviation of Rs 24,000. Its coefficient of variation (standard deviation / mean), as a measure of risk per rupee of expected return, is:
e: Coefficient of variation = standard deviation / mean = 24000 / 120000 = 0.20, measuring risk per rupee of expected return.

q: A project's net cash inflow in a year is estimated at Rs 5,00,000 with a probability of 0.6 and Rs 2,50,000 with a probability of 0.4. The expected (probability-weighted) cash inflow is:
For one and the same project appraised at a positive discount rate, the discounted payback period will always be:

options.A: Longer than the ordinary (simple) payback period, because each inflow is reduced to its present value before being set against the outlay
options.B: Shorter than the ordinary (simple) payback period
options.C: Exactly equal to the ordinary (simple) payback period
options.D: Zero, because discounting eliminates the payback concept

e: In discounted payback each inflow is first reduced to present value, so a larger undiscounted total is needed to recover the outlay and the discounted payback is always longer than the simple payback at a positive discount rate.

q: Rs 50,000 is set aside at the end of each year for 3 years at 10% compound interest. The accumulated (future) value of this annuity at the end of Year 3 (future value annuity factor for 3 years at 10% = 3.310) is:
e: Future value of the annuity = 50000 x 3.310 = Rs 165500, using the future value annuity factor for 3 years at 10 percent.

q: Two mutually exclusive projects have conflicting rankings: Project X has the higher Net Present Value and Project Y the higher Internal Rate of Return. Funds are available for either project. The project to be chosen is:

options.A: Project Y, because a rate of return is always preferable to an absolute amount
options.B: Either project, because both the criteria are equally valid in all cases
options.C: Neither project, because the two criteria do not agree
options.D: Project X, because the object is to maximise the absolute addition to wealth, which the Net Present Value measures directly

e: NPV measures the absolute addition to wealth directly, so where NPV and IRR conflict for mutually exclusive projects and funds are available, the higher-NPV project X should be chosen.

q: In the cash flows of a project, the working capital invested in it is treated as:

options.A: An annual revenue expense of the project throughout its life
options.B: A cash outflow when it is invested (at the start, or when it increases) and a cash inflow when it is recovered at the end; it is not depreciated and its recovery is not treated as income
options.C: A part of the salvage value of the plant and machinery
options.D: A sunk cost, to be ignored in the appraisal

e: Working capital is a cash outflow when invested at the start or increased, and a cash inflow when recovered at the end; it is not depreciated and its recovery is not income.

q: An enterprise has cash in hand of Rs 45,000, a bank balance of Rs 75,000 and marketable securities of Rs 1,80,000. Its current liabilities are Rs 10,00,000. Its absolute liquid (super quick) ratio is:
e: Absolute liquid assets = 45000 + 75000 + 180000 = Rs 300000. Absolute liquid ratio = 300000 / 1000000 = 0.3 to 1.

q: The proprietors' funds of an enterprise are Rs 17,50,000 and its total assets are Rs 25,00,000. Its proprietary ratio is:
e: Proprietary ratio = proprietors funds / total assets = 1750000 / 2500000 = 0.70.

q: The long-term debt of an enterprise is Rs 13,50,000 and its shareholders' funds are Rs 18,00,000. Its debt-equity ratio is:
e: Debt-equity ratio = long-term debt / shareholders funds = 1350000 / 1800000 = 0.75 to 1.

q: The cost of goods sold of an enterprise is Rs 16,80,000. Its opening inventory is Rs 2,00,000 and its closing inventory is Rs 2,80,000. Its inventory (stock) turnover ratio is:

options.A: 6 times
options.B: 7 times
options.C: 8.4 times
options.D: 5 times

e: Average inventory = (200000 + 280000) / 2 = Rs 240000. Inventory turnover = 1680000 / 240000 = 7 times.

q: The net credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 36,00,000 and its average trade debtors are Rs 4,50,000. The debtors velocity (average collection period expressed in months) is:

options.A: 1.5 months
options.B: 8 months
options.C: 3 months
options.D: 6 months

e: Debtors turnover = 3600000 / 450000 = 8 times, so average collection period = 12 / 8 = 1.5 months.

q: The profit after tax of an enterprise is Rs 3,30,000 and its shareholders' funds are Rs 15,00,000. Its return on shareholders' funds is:
e: Return on shareholders funds = profit after tax / shareholders funds x 100 = 330000 / 1500000 x 100 = 22 percent.

q: The net profit after tax of a company is Rs 12,60,000 and the preference dividend payable is Rs 60,000. The company has 2,00,000 equity shares. Its Earnings Per Share is:
e: Earnings for equity = 1260000 - 60000 = Rs 1200000. EPS = 1200000 / 200000 shares = Rs 6.00 per share.

q: The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 9,00,000 and its interest payable is Rs 2,00,000. Its interest coverage ratio is:

options.A: 3 times
options.B: 4.5 times
options.C: 2.5 times
options.D: 0.22 times

e: Interest coverage ratio = profit before interest and tax / interest = 900000 / 200000 = 4.5 times.

q: The fixed assets ratio (net fixed assets / long-term funds, i.e., capital employed) of an enterprise exceeds 1. This indicates that:

options.A: A part of the fixed assets has been financed out of short-term (current) funds, which is an unsound financial position
options.B: The fixed assets are fully financed by long-term funds, with a margin to spare
options.C: The enterprise owns no fixed assets at all
options.D: The current assets of the enterprise exceed its current liabilities

e: A fixed assets ratio above 1 means net fixed assets exceed long-term funds, so the excess must have been financed from short-term current funds, which is financially unsound.

q: The net sales of an enterprise are Rs 45,00,000 and its capital employed is Rs 18,00,000. Its capital employed turnover ratio is:

options.A: 0.4 times
options.B: 4 times
options.C: 2.5 times
options.D: 1.8 times

e: Capital employed turnover = net sales / capital employed = 4500000 / 1800000 = 2.5 times.

q: Ratios computed from the balance sheet of a single date can be distorted by 'window dressing'. An analyst can reduce this distortion by:

options.A: Using only the balances as on the year-end date
options.B: Ignoring the cash flow statement of the enterprise
options.C: Comparing the enterprise only with its own past position
options.D: Using average balances over the period and examining the transactions immediately before and after the balance-sheet date for year-end adjustments that are soon reversed

e: Window dressing at the balance-sheet date is reduced by using average balances over the period and scrutinising transactions just before and after that date for year-end adjustments that are soon reversed.

q: In ratio analysis, 'impersonal standards' of comparison are those which are:

options.A: Based on the past ratios of the same enterprise itself
options.B: Derived from outside the enterprise, such as industry averages or the ratios of leading competitors, and applied as common benchmarks
options.C: Fixed personally by the manager of the enterprise
options.D: Computed without using the figures of any enterprise

e: Impersonal standards are external benchmarks derived outside the enterprise, such as industry averages or leading competitors ratios, against which the enterprise is commonly compared.

q: An enterprise has current assets of Rs 6,00,000 and current liabilities of Rs 4,00,000 (current ratio 1.5 : 1). It purchases stock of Rs 2,00,000 on credit. Its current ratio will:

options.A: Fall to about 1.33 : 1
options.B: Rise to about 1.67 : 1
options.C: Remain unchanged at 1.5 : 1
options.D: Become 2 : 1

e: After the credit purchase, current assets = 600000 + 200000 = Rs 800000 and current liabilities = 400000 + 200000 = Rs 600000, so current ratio = 800000 / 600000 = about 1.33 to 1, a fall because the ratio was above 1.

q: An enterprise has stock of Rs 3,60,000, trade debtors of Rs 2,90,000, cash and bank balances of Rs 85,000 and prepaid expenses of Rs 25,000. Its current liabilities are Rs 3,00,000. Its quick (liquid) ratio is:
e: Quick assets exclude stock and prepaid expenses, so quick assets = 290000 + 85000 = Rs 375000. Quick ratio = 375000 / 300000 = 1.25 to 1.

q: The total debt (long-term debt plus current liabilities) of an enterprise is Rs 9,60,000 and its total assets are Rs 24,00,000. Its debt ratio is:
e: Debt ratio = total debt / total assets = 960000 / 2400000 = 0.4.

q: The annual credit purchases of an enterprise are Rs 21,90,000 and its average trade creditors are Rs 3,00,000. Its creditors turnover ratio is:

options.A: 0.14 times
options.B: 5 times
options.C: 7.3 times
options.D: 10 times

e: Creditors turnover ratio = annual credit purchases / average trade creditors = 2190000 / 300000 = 7.3 times.

q: A single ratio, read in isolation, can mislead the analyst mainly because:

options.A: The position of an enterprise is the joint result of many factors, so a ratio acquires meaning only when read with the related ratios, the past trends and the circumstances of the enterprise
options.B: Ratios can be computed only by the statutory auditors
options.C: Ratios are always expressed as percentages
options.D: A ratio necessarily requires figures of two different years

e: An enterprise position results from many interacting factors, so a single ratio misleads unless read with related ratios, past trends and the circumstances of the enterprise.

q: Two enterprises both have a current ratio of 2 : 1. In Enterprise X most of the current assets consist of stock, while in Enterprise Y most of them consist of debtors and cash. Other things being equal:

options.A: Both the enterprises are equally liquid
options.B: Enterprise X is more liquid than Enterprise Y
options.C: Neither enterprise has any working capital
options.D: Enterprise Y is more liquid than Enterprise X, because stock is the least liquid of the current assets and may take time to be sold and realised

e: Stock is the least liquid current asset and takes time to sell and realise, so Enterprise Y holding mainly debtors and cash is more liquid than Enterprise X despite both having a current ratio of 2 to 1.

q: Return on Equity (shareholders' funds) will normally differ from the Return on Capital Employed of the same enterprise mainly because:

options.A: Return on Capital Employed is computed on sales, while Return on Equity is computed on assets
options.B: Return on Capital Employed is measured by the profit before interest and tax on all the long-term funds, while Return on Equity is measured by the profit after interest and tax on the owners' funds alone, so the effect of borrowing (leverage) and of tax falls on the latter
options.C: Return on Equity ignores the profit of the enterprise altogether
options.D: The two returns are always equal in every enterprise

e: ROCE uses profit before interest and tax on all long-term funds, while ROE uses profit after interest and tax on owners funds alone, so borrowing leverage and tax affect ROE but not ROCE in the same way.

q: The gross profit ratio of an enterprise has improved during the year, but its net profit ratio has fallen. The most likely explanation is:

options.A: The cost of goods sold has risen faster than the sales
options.B: The sales of the enterprise have fallen to zero
options.C: Operating expenses, interest or tax have risen sufficiently to more than absorb the improvement in the gross profit
options.D: Preference dividend has been deducted in arriving at the gross profit

e: If gross profit ratio improves but net profit ratio falls, operating expenses, interest or tax must have risen enough to more than absorb the gross profit improvement.

q: An enterprise which maintains a very high current ratio by holding large idle cash balances and excessive stock may suffer on the profitability side because:

options.A: Funds locked up in low-yielding or idle current assets earn little or nothing, depressing the return on the capital employed
options.B: A high current ratio always indicates insolvency of the enterprise
options.C: Creditors refuse to supply materials to such an enterprise
options.D: Its fixed assets have necessarily to be sold off

e: Large idle cash and excessive stock lock funds in low-yielding current assets that earn little or nothing, depressing the return on capital employed despite a high current ratio.

q: In computing the debtors turnover ratio, only the net credit sales should be used (in place of the total sales) because:

options.A: Cash sales are never recorded in the books of account
options.B: Total sales include the drawings of the proprietor
options.C: Debtors arise from cash sales as well as from credit sales
options.D: Debtors arise only from credit sales; including cash sales would overstate the turnover and understate the true collection period

e: Debtors arise only from credit sales, so only net credit sales belong in the debtors turnover ratio; including cash sales would overstate turnover and understate the true collection period.

q: In most manufacturing enterprises, the sales budget is regarded as the foundation on which the other functional budgets are built, mainly because:

options.A: The level of production, purchases, labour and cash requirements all depend upon the volume of sales expected to be achieved
options.B: The sales department is always the largest department of the enterprise
options.C: Sales are the only item appearing in the budgeted profit and loss account
options.D: The sales budget is the last budget to be approved by the budget committee

e: The sales budget is the foundation budget because expected sales volume determines the required production, purchases, labour and cash, so all other functional budgets are built upon it.

q: The capital expenditure budget of an enterprise requires particularly careful preparation and approval at a high level mainly because:

options.A: Capital expenditure is incurred afresh every month in the same amount
options.B: It commits large sums for long periods on assets whose cost is largely irreversible once incurred, and it must be coordinated with the cash budget and the sources of long-term finance
options.C: It covers only the repairs and maintenance of existing plant
options.D: It is prepared only after the actual expenditure has been incurred

e: Capital expenditure commits large sums for long periods on assets whose cost is largely irreversible, so it needs careful high-level approval and coordination with the cash budget and long-term finance sources.

q: A manpower budget of an enterprise primarily shows:

options.A: The total wages payable to the workers during the budget period only
options.B: The cash required for payment of gratuity at the end of the year
options.C: The number and categories of personnel, by grade and department, required to carry out the budgeted programme, together with the cost of employing them
options.D: The names of the employees to be promoted during the budget period

e: A manpower budget shows the number and categories of personnel by grade and department needed for the budgeted programme, together with the cost of employing them, not merely total wages.

q: A newly appointed budget officer wishes to ascertain the timetable for submission of departmental estimates, the forms to be used and the officials responsible for each budget. He should consult the budget manual, because one of its main contents is:

options.A: The audited financial statements of the previous year
options.B: The standard cost card for every product of the enterprise
options.C: The list of customers to whom credit may be allowed
options.D: The budget calendar and procedure, setting out the stages of budget preparation, the responsibilities of each official and the dates by which each stage is to be completed

e: The budget manual contains the budget calendar and procedure, setting out the stages of preparation, the responsibilities of each official and the dates for completing each stage.

q: A departmental manager deliberately understates the revenue expected from his department and pads the estimates of its expenses, so that the budget targets become easy for him to achieve. This practice is known as:

options.A: Building budgetary slack into the estimates
options.B: Zero-based budgeting
options.C: Flexing of the budget
options.D: Management by exception

e: Deliberately understating expected revenue and padding expenses to make targets easy to achieve is building budgetary slack into the estimates.

q: An enterprise always keeps a budget ready for the next twelve months: as each quarter ends, the budget for that quarter is dropped and a budget for a fresh quarter at the end of the period is added. Such a budget is an example of:

options.A: A fixed budget
options.B: A rolling or continuous budget, which maintains a constant planning horizon ahead
options.C: A cash budget
options.D: A supplementary budget

e: A budget that always covers the next twelve months, dropping the elapsed quarter and adding a fresh quarter at the end, is a rolling or continuous budget maintaining a constant planning horizon.

q: Under activity-based budgeting, the budget for a department is built up primarily by:

options.A: Increasing the previous year's figures by a uniform percentage for inflation
options.B: Taking the actual expenditure of the corresponding month of the last year as the base
options.C: Identifying the activities to be performed, estimating the demand for each activity and the resources it will consume on the basis of its cost drivers
options.D: Dividing the total available funds equally among all the departments

e: Activity-based budgeting identifies the activities to be performed, estimates demand for each activity and resources consumed based on its cost drivers, instead of merely inflating past figures.

q: In deciding whether a particular budget variance reported to management should be investigated further, the sound guiding principle is that:

options.A: Every variance, however small, must be investigated in full detail
options.B: Only favourable variances should ever be investigated
options.C: Variances should be investigated only at the end of the financial year
options.D: A variance should be investigated only when the expected benefit from investigation and corrective action is likely to exceed the cost of the investigation

e: A variance should be investigated only when the expected benefit from investigation and corrective action is likely to exceed the cost of investigating it.

q: In the sequence of preparation of the master budget, the document that is normally completed last, summarising the effect of all the functional budgets on the financial position of the enterprise, is:

options.A: The budgeted balance sheet
options.B: The sales budget
options.C: The production budget
options.D: The raw material purchase budget

e: The budgeted balance sheet is completed last in the master budget because it summarises the effect of all functional budgets on the financial position of the enterprise.

q: A cash budget for a month shows an opening cash balance of Rs 65,000, estimated receipts of Rs 3,40,000 and estimated payments of Rs 3,75,000. The closing cash balance for the month will be:
e: Closing cash balance = opening balance + receipts - payments = 65000 + 340000 - 375000 = Rs 30000.

q: Production of 30,000 units is budgeted, and each unit requires 3 kg of a material. The opening stock of the material is 7,000 kg and the closing stock is to be raised to 9,000 kg. The quantity of material to be purchased is:
e: Material required = 30000 x 3 = 90000 kg. Purchases = 90000 + closing stock 9000 - opening stock 7000 = 92000 kg.

q: The direct labour budget of a factory is derived mainly from:

options.A: The selling overhead budget of the marketing department
options.B: The cash budget of the enterprise
options.C: The capital expenditure budget for new plant
options.D: The production budget, by applying the standard labour time required per unit and the wage rates for the grades of labour to be employed

e: The direct labour budget is derived from the production budget by applying standard labour time per unit and wage rates for the grades of labour to be employed.

q: The selling and distribution overhead budget is most directly dependent upon:

options.A: The sales budget, since items like salesmen's commission, advertising linked to sales campaigns and carriage outwards vary with the budgeted sales activity
options.B: The balance sheet of the previous year
options.C: The number of shares issued by the enterprise
options.D: The depreciation charged on factory plant

e: Selling and distribution overheads like commission, campaign advertising and carriage outwards vary with budgeted sales activity, so this budget depends most directly on the sales budget.

q: The standard hours required for the actual output of a department are 9,600 hours, while the actual hours worked are 8,000 hours. The efficiency ratio of the department is:
e: Efficiency ratio = standard hours / actual hours x 100 = 9600 / 8000 x 100 = 120 percent.

q: A budget centre, for the purpose of budgetary control, is best described as:

options.A: The office where the budget committee holds its meetings
options.B: The officer who approves the budget of the enterprise
options.C: A section, department or part of the enterprise for which a separate budget is prepared and against which control is exercised
options.D: The bank account through which all budgeted payments are made

e: A budget centre is a section, department or part of the enterprise for which a separate budget is prepared and against which budgetary control is exercised.

q: Budgeted sales of a product are 88,000 units. The opening stock of finished goods is 11,000 units and the closing stock is to be raised to 14,000 units. The production budget should provide for production of:

options.A: 85,000 units
options.B: 88,000 units
options.D: 91,000 units

e: Production = budgeted sales + closing stock - opening stock = 88000 + 14000 - 11000 = 91000 units.

q: A budget prepared with the active involvement of the managers who will be responsible for achieving it, rather than imposed from above, generally has the advantage that:

options.A: It improves the commitment and motivation of those managers towards achieving the targets, though care is needed to guard against slack being built into their estimates
options.B: It removes the need for any subsequent comparison of actuals with the budget
options.C: It guarantees that the targets will always be achieved
options.D: It makes the budget committee unnecessary

e: Participative budgeting improves commitment and motivation of managers responsible for the targets, though care is needed to guard against slack being built into their estimates.

q: The budget period, that is, the length of the period covered by a budget, is mainly determined by:

options.A: The number of departments in the enterprise
options.B: The nature of the business and the purpose of the budget, operating budgets commonly covering a year broken into months, while capital budgets may extend over several years
options.C: The date on which the auditors complete their audit
options.D: The life of the longest-serving employee of the enterprise

e: The budget period is determined mainly by the nature of the business and purpose of the budget; operating budgets commonly cover a year in months while capital budgets may span several years.

q: In a manufacturing concern, raw materials are held for 45 days, the production process takes 15 days, finished goods are held for 30 days and debtors are collected in 60 days. Suppliers allow 45 days' credit. The length of the net operating cycle is:

options.A: 150 days
options.B: 195 days
options.C: 105 days
options.D: 90 days

e: Gross operating cycle = 45 + 15 + 30 + 60 = 150 days. Net operating cycle = 150 - suppliers credit 45 = 105 days.

q: Working capital leverage refers to the effect on the profitability and risk of an enterprise of:

options.A: Employing more long-term debt in the capital structure
options.B: Financing a given level of current assets with a larger proportion of current liabilities, which tends to raise the return but also increases the risk of the enterprise
options.C: Holding the whole of the working capital in the form of cash
options.D: Leasing fixed assets instead of purchasing them

e: Working capital leverage is the effect of financing a given level of current assets with a larger proportion of current liabilities, which tends to raise return but also increases risk.

q: The risk-return trade-off in working capital management implies that, other things being equal:

options.A: A higher level of working capital raises both the risk and the return of the enterprise
options.B: The level of working capital has no effect on either risk or return
options.C: A lower level of working capital lowers both the risk and the return of the enterprise
options.D: A higher level of working capital lowers the risk of interruption and default but also lowers profitability, because more funds remain locked up in less-yielding current assets

e: A higher level of working capital lowers the risk of interruption and default but also lowers profitability, because more funds stay locked up in less-yielding current assets; this is the risk-return trade-off.

q: An enterprise keeps a part of its cash balance to meet unexpected payments, such as an unforeseen repair bill or a sudden demand from a creditor. The motive for holding cash illustrated by this is the:

options.A: Transaction motive
options.B: Precautionary motive
options.C: Speculative motive
options.D: Compensating motive

e: Cash held to meet unexpected payments such as an unforeseen repair bill or a sudden creditor demand is held for the precautionary motive.

q: Cash that is temporarily surplus to the immediate requirements of an enterprise is generally invested in marketable securities because such securities:

options.A: Are highly liquid and low-risk and can be converted back into cash quickly when needed, while earning some return instead of lying idle
options.B: Can never fall in value under any circumstances
options.C: Are not required to be shown in the accounts of the enterprise
options.D: Always earn a higher return than the main business of the enterprise

e: Temporarily surplus cash is invested in marketable securities because they are highly liquid and low-risk, can be converted back to cash quickly, and earn some return instead of lying idle.

q: The credit policy of an enterprise is administered through three main variables. These are:

options.A: Purchase price, wage rate and rent
options.B: Fixed costs, variable costs and semi-variable costs
options.C: Credit standards, credit terms (including the credit period and cash discount) and the collection policy
options.D: Opening stock, purchases and closing stock

e: Credit policy is administered through credit standards, credit terms including credit period and cash discount, and the collection policy.

q: Shortage costs in relation to inventory held as a part of working capital include:

options.A: The interest on the funds locked up in the stock held
options.B: The insurance premium paid for covering the stock against fire
options.C: The rent of the godown in which the stock is stored
options.D: The loss of contribution from sales lost through stock-outs, the cost of interrupted production and the loss of customer goodwill

e: Shortage or stock-out costs include lost contribution from sales lost, cost of interrupted production and loss of customer goodwill, unlike carrying costs such as interest, insurance and godown rent.

q: Under the ABC system of inventory control applied as a part of working capital management, the tightest control and the most careful estimation of requirements are exercised over:

options.A: Category C items, which form a large proportion of the total value of stock
options.B: Category A items, which are few in number but account for a large proportion of the total value of inventory
options.C: All items of stock equally, whatever their value
options.D: Only the items that have become obsolete

e: In ABC control, Category A items are few in number but account for a large proportion of total inventory value, so they receive the tightest control and most careful estimation of requirements.

q: The current assets of an enterprise increased from Rs 8,20,000 to Rs 9,10,000 during a year, while its current liabilities increased from Rs 4,60,000 to Rs 5,30,000. The net change in its working capital during the year is:

options.A: An increase of Rs 20,000
options.B: An increase of Rs 90,000
options.C: A decrease of Rs 20,000
options.D: An increase of Rs 1,60,000

e: Working capital first year = 820000 - 460000 = Rs 360000; second year = 910000 - 530000 = Rs 380000. Net change = 380000 - 360000 = an increase of Rs 20000.

q: The annual operating cost of an enterprise is Rs 54,75,000, reckoning a year of 365 days. Its operating cycle is 64 days. On the operating-cycle method, the working capital required is:
e: Cost per day = 5475000 / 365 = Rs 15000. Working capital required = 15000 x 64 days = Rs 960000 on the operating-cycle method.

q: An enterprise has an inventory conversion period of 55 days, a receivables collection period of 45 days and a payables deferral period of 40 days. Its cash conversion cycle is:

options.A: 100 days
options.B: 140 days
options.C: 15 days
options.D: 60 days

e: Cash conversion cycle = inventory period + receivables period - payables period = 55 + 45 - 40 = 60 days.

q: The current assets of an enterprise are Rs 14,40,000 and its current ratio is 2.4 : 1. Its net working capital is:
e: Current liabilities = 1440000 / 2.4 = Rs 600000. Net working capital = 1440000 - 600000 = Rs 840000.

q: Sources of finance described as spontaneous sources of working capital are those which:

options.A: Require a formal application to a bank in every case
options.B: Are available only from the Government
options.C: Arise automatically in the course of operations, such as trade credit from suppliers and accrued wages and expenses
options.D: Are raised by the issue of shares to the public

e: Spontaneous sources arise automatically in the course of operations, such as trade credit from suppliers and accrued wages and expenses, without any formal financing arrangement.

q: An enterprise is said to be overtrading when it:

options.A: Expands its sales and operations rapidly without a corresponding increase in its working capital, so that it becomes overstretched, delays payment to creditors and risks failure despite making profits
options.B: Holds far more working capital than its level of operations requires
options.C: Sells its goods only for cash
options.D: Maintains a current ratio well above the level customary in its industry

e: Overtrading is expanding sales and operations rapidly without a matching increase in working capital, leaving the firm overstretched, delaying creditors and risking failure despite profits.

q: If an enterprise lengthens the credit period allowed to its customers, the most likely combined effect is that:

options.A: Sales will fall and the investment in receivables will also fall
options.B: There will be no change in sales, receivables or bad debts
options.C: The cash conversion cycle will become shorter
options.D: Sales may increase, but the funds blocked in receivables, the collection effort and the risk of bad debts will also increase

e: Lengthening the credit period may increase sales, but it also increases funds blocked in receivables, collection effort and the risk of bad debts.

q: Where provision for taxation is treated as a non-current liability in preparing a fund flow statement, the income-tax actually paid during the year is shown as:

options.A: A source of funds
options.B: An application of funds, the provision made during the year being added back in computing the funds from operations
options.C: A reduction of the share capital
options.D: No entry at all in the fund flow statement

e: When provision for taxation is treated as non-current, tax actually paid is an application of funds, while the provision made during the year is added back in computing funds from operations.

q: Interim dividend paid during the year is dealt with in the fund flow statement by:

options.A: Treating it as an operating expense of the year only
options.B: Ignoring it altogether, since it is only an interim payment
options.C: Showing the amount paid as an application of funds, after adding it back in the adjusted profit and loss account for computing the funds from operations
options.D: Showing the amount paid as a source of funds

e: Interim dividend paid is shown as an application of funds, after adding it back in the adjusted profit and loss account when computing funds from operations.

q: An enterprise issues equity shares directly to the vendor in consideration for machinery purchased from him, no cash passing between the parties. In the fund flow statement, this transaction appears as:

options.A: Neither a source nor an application of funds, because it involves only two non-current items and causes no change in working capital
options.B: A source of funds equal to the value of the machinery
options.C: An application of funds equal to the value of the machinery
options.D: Both a source and an application, increasing the working capital

e: Shares issued directly to a vendor for machinery involve only two non-current items, share capital and machinery, with no change in working capital, so the transaction is neither a source nor an application of funds.

q: Under Accounting Standard 3 (AS-3), in the cash flow statement of a non-financial enterprise, interest received on investments is classified as a cash flow from:

options.A: Operating activities
options.B: Financing activities
options.C: Operating activities if the amount is small, and financing activities otherwise
options.D: Investing activities

e: Under AS-3, for a non-financial enterprise, interest received on investments is a return on investment and is classified as a cash flow from investing activities.

q: In a cash flow statement, a refund of income-tax received by an enterprise is generally classified as a cash flow from:

options.A: Investing activities, in every case
options.B: Operating activities, unless it can be specifically identified with an investing or a financing transaction
options.C: Financing activities, in every case
options.D: No activity, because a refund is not a cash flow

e: A refund of income-tax is generally an operating cash flow, unless it can be specifically identified with an investing or a financing transaction.

q: An enterprise receives an insurance claim in respect of a factory building destroyed by fire. In its cash flow statement, the amount received is classified as a cash flow from:

options.A: Operating activities, as a part of the normal trading receipts
options.B: Financing activities, as a receipt from the insurers
options.C: Investing activities, being compensation for the loss of a fixed asset
options.D: No activity, because the claim is an extraordinary item

e: An insurance claim for a factory building destroyed by fire compensates for loss of a fixed asset, so the amount received is classified as a cash flow from investing activities.

q: A fixed asset having a book value of Rs 80,000 is sold for Rs 95,000. In the fund flow statement, the amount shown as a source of funds in respect of this transaction is:

options.A: Rs 95,000, being the sale proceeds received
options.B: Rs 15,000, being the profit on the sale
options.C: Rs 80,000, being the book value of the asset
options.D: Nil, because the sale of a fixed asset is not a source of funds

e: Sale of a fixed asset is a source of funds to the full extent of proceeds received, Rs 95000; the profit of Rs 15000 is separately adjusted in funds from operations.
